newsitem.title: USA: INTERVIEW - Kodak sees entertainment-imaging growth.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Kodak sees entertainment-imaging growth.

text.p: Eastman Kodak Co Chief Financial Officer Harry Kavetas on Thursday hailed the company's cost-cutting moves in 1996 and predicted growth this year in Kodak's entertainment imaging business.
In an interview with Reuters, Kavetas declined to provide specific growth estimates for the business, whose sales jumped about 20 percent in 1996.

The business, which produces special effects for the film industry and involves traditional photographic imaging as well as digital imaging, will prove to be an "exciting area" for the company in 1997, Kavetas said.
In 1996, Kodak did "well in working with the movie industry," he said.

In anticipation of further growth, Kodak last year increased investments to expand the capacity of its motion picture facilities, Kavetas said. The program included a $200 million film manufacturing investment last May.
Kavetas said Kodak would also boost its advertising and sales promotion spending, as well as spending on research and development.
"I'm confident we'll increase our expenditures in both areas," he said, although declined to be more specific.
The company spent $1.25 billion on advertising and sales promotions in 1996 and $1.28 billion on research and development, he said.

Kodak's increasing focus on entertainment imaging, among other areas, was reflected in its agreement last autumn to sell of its Office Imaging unit to Danka Business Systems Plc for $684 million. Kodak is also restructuring its operations.
In 1996, the company recorded an after-tax loss of $252 million for the sale of the Office Imaging business, and an after-tax loss of $256 million for restructuring, the company said on Thursday.
Earlier Thursday, Kodak posted fourth-quarter earnings of $0.49 a share, including charges, compared with $0.80 in the year-ago period.

Prudential Securities analyst Alexander Henderson said that Kodak's restructuring moves, as well as its intention to refrain from increasing its workforce this year, could only improve margins. That in turn means higher earnings, he added.
"Well, you can reach that conclusion," Kavetas said, although he again declined specific comment. "We as a matter of policy don't forecast earnings," he added.
Earlier in the day, Prudential raised its 1997 earnings estimate for Kodak to $5.15 per share from $5.00, and its 1998 estimate to $5.95 per share from $5.80.
Prudential also reiterated a "buy" on the stock and raised its 12-month price target to $100 per share from $95.
The company's 1996 earnings rose to $3.82 per share from $3.67 in 1995.
Kodak's stock was up as much as 4-1/2 at 85-3/4 on the New York Stock Exchange Thursday.
